newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Politics seen behind power cuts in Russia Far East.
newsitem.headline: Politics seen behind power cuts in Russia Far East.

text.p: Politics, not fuel, were the real cause of the energy crisis in Russia's Far East, First Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Sergei Kiriyenko said on Tuesday.

"The main cause of the crisis has a more political character than being a real energy crisis," he told a news briefing, adding that he did not expect any more power supply interruptions in the region during the sumer months.

Kiriyenko was reporting on the results of a ministry commission in Moscow charged with looking into the energy crisis in the far east of the country, which left the Vladivostock district without power for over 20 hours a day last month.

Kiriyenko said the shortfall of coal, the main feedstock for power generators in the far eastern region of Primorsky Krai, was 10 to 12 percent of total supply, and during the summer months there should be no energy crisis at all.
"In Primorsky Krai the energy shortage is not very great -- the problem there is a political one," he said.
One of the main causes of electricity supply cuts in the region was a decision to keep electricity prices artificially low during the last year and a half, Kiriyenko said.
First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, who is also Fuel and Energy Minister, said last week that higher energy tariffs were needed to end the power cuts.
But Primorsky's populist governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko has resisted price hikes, saying they would cripple local industry.
Nemtsov said Moscow might sack Nazdratenko over his handling of the crisis, but Kiriyenko hinted that such drastic measures may have been avoided.

"The commission has fully carried out its plan, which was agreed with the government without any need for political measures, and without those extreme measures towards which we are constantly being pushed," he said.
He would not name names but said "mistakes and incompetence" had plagued the region's energy sector in recent months.
But despite administrative shortcomings in the handling of the crisis, further power cuts in the region were unlikely during the summer months, Kiriyenko said.

"The main thing is that there were no interruptions to electricity supplies during the work of the commission, and we have created all the conditions to ensure that there will be no interruptions until winter," he said.
Kiriyenko said coal stocks at the region's power utility, Dalenergo, had risen to 250,000 tonnes from nil at the time the commission began its work in the region.
The region's major hydro-electric station also had 123,000 tonnes of coal set aside, he added.
He said further preparations were needed in Primorsky Krai, and across the country as a whole, in order to avoid energy crises during the winter months.
The commission's experience in addressing the energy crisis in Russia's Far East could be used as the basis for resolving similar issues in other regions.

Kiriyenko said one proposal being considered was to turn existing local energy commissions into local agents of the Federal Energy Commission (FEC). The FEC was set up to introduce more market economy elements into energy exports and tariffs.
